The statement signals a strong labor market and low unemployment—conditions typically associated with above-trend output via the inverse unemployment–output relationship (Okun-type regularities; see references noting the Unemployment Rate’s inverse relationship with Real GDP). In New Keynesian frameworks, low unemployment would normally raise inflation pressures through the Phillips curve, but with expectations anchored and inflation below target—as the release notes—price pressures tend to build only gradually (Galí and Gertler 1999; Woodford 2003; Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans 2005; references on inflation expectations and inertia). Monetary easing also supports continued employment gains and activity (literature documenting monetary policy’s effects on real GDP and output fluctuations, e.g., Sims-type VAR evidence and the cited “Monetary Policy Affects real GDP” references). Balancing these, the tone is clearly positive but not exuberant, given broader uncertainties and weak business fixed investment emphasized in the release and in the investment literature linking investment to financing conditions and rates (e.g., Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; references on investment’s dependence on interest rates and internal funds).
